draft.title: Changes of state
card: A change of state happens when a substance gains or loses heat energy. The particles stay the same. Only their movement and spacing change.
Adding heat makes particles move faster and spread out. A solid melts into a liquid. A liquid boils into a gas.
Losing heat makes particles move more slowly and come closer together. A gas condenses into a liquid. A liquid freezes into a solid.
Water melts and freezes at 0 °C, and boils and condenses at 100 °C. Ice and steam are both made of the same water particles.
draft.remember: Heat in speeds particles up. Heat out slows them down.

a.q: Steam touches a cold window and turns into drops of water. What happens to the water particles?
opts: They lose heat, slow down and move closer together
They gain heat, speed up and move further apart
They lose heat, speed up and move closer together
They gain heat, slow down and move further apart
a.why: Steam turning to liquid is condensing, which happens when heat is lost. The particles slow down and come closer together. Gaining heat would make them speed up and spread out, which is boiling.
a.clue: Condensing is a gas becoming a liquid. Is heat added or lost?

b.q: Liam heats a block of wax in a pan. It becomes a runny liquid. Which statement best explains this?
opts: The wax particles gained heat, moved faster and spread out
The wax particles gained heat and changed into new particles
The wax particles lost heat and slid past each other
The wax particles gained heat and became larger in size
b.why: Heat makes the particles move faster and spread out, so the solid melts. The particles themselves do not change, because a change of state only changes movement and spacing. Losing heat would make wax freeze, not melt.
b.clue: The particles stay the same. Think about what heat changes.

a.best: They lose heat, slow down and move closer together

b.best: The wax particles gained heat, moved faster and spread out

problems.detail: 'Water ... boils and condenses at 100 °C' suggests water vapour only condenses at 100 °C. Condensation happens at much lower temperatures, including the cold window in question a. Boiling at 100 °C is also only true at sea-level pressure. Say water boils at 100 °C at sea level, and that water vapour can condense at lower temperatures.

The card says losing heat makes particles come closer together as a liquid freezes, then uses water as its example. Water is the well-known exception: ice particles are further apart than in liquid water, which is why ice floats. Add a brief note or use a different example.
Why (b) says 'Losing heat would make wax freeze, not melt.' The wax starts as a solid, so losing heat would just keep it solid. Freezing applies to a liquid.

check.summary: Both questions have a single clear right answer that matches the intended one. The card wrongly implies water vapour condenses only at 100 °C, and it uses water as its freezing example even though ice is the exception to particles moving closer together. The why for (b) also misuses 'freeze' for a solid.
